transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-01-15 15:30 UTC | Duration 48m | Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Brandon (Redwood SE), Ellen (Redwood CSM); Avery, Rosa, Devon, Samir (ZenPath)

Summary: quick recap at top, then long transcript.

00:00:00 - Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to do a focused deep dive on your rerank pipeline and embedding economics, is the agenda still the same?
00:00:08 - Avery: Yeah that's right, mostly focused on latency SLO and cost curve. We run a two-stage retrieve + rerank. Retrieval uses an ANN layer (HNSW) and then a small cross-encoder rerank stage, but we're considering moving some of the rerank work to a single-pass embed + dot product flow to save costs.
00:00:27 - Brandon: Cool. Can you give a short baseline? p95 latency currently, qps, vector dimension, etc.
00:00:34 - Samir: Sure, current production: 100 rps peak, p95 end-to-end is about 220ms. We use 1024-d vectors from an open model, batch size at inference is effectively 16 on our side, but the reranker is run per-candidate so it spikes. We want to hit p95 ~ 100ms, ideally 80-120ms.
00:00:56 - Rosa: And infra-wise we are in a VPC with restricted egress, prefer on-prem for pilot. KMS is required for keys.
00:01:05 - Brandon: ok, good context. For the embedding/rerank tradeoff there are a few levers: vector dims, model size/quantization, batching, KV cache (prefix caching of key/value state for decoder-style models), and routing to dedicated pools.
00:01:21 - Avery: Walk me through the dim tradeoffs — we saw papers but curious for perf/cost in practice.
00:01:28 - Brandon: Right. Short version: smaller dims lower memory and compute for ANN and dot-prod cost, but can reduce accuracy for rerank. For throughput, a 128-d vs 1024-d vector reduces storage and network transfer by ~8x. On the runtime, per-token cost is smaller because embedding generator is smaller. But the actual perf depends on whether you do a single forward for embedding vector (cheap) or cross-encoder rerank (expensive).
00:01:55 - Maya: To add: our Optimize tooling can suggest a dim profile by workload — we ran quantized 256-d prototype for another customer and saw 2.4x cost reduction with <1.5% NDCG drop.
00:02:08 - Devon: That's promising. What's the story for the KV cache — our rerank is stateless but we might reuse prefix caches between queries for context reuse.
00:02:16 - Brandon: In Redwood's serving runtime, KV cache is primarily for autoregressive decoders. For embedding flows it shows up if you have stateful contexts or reuse earlier sequence prefixes. In rerank pipelines the big win is reusing candidate embeddings in a cache or using a hotlist prefix for repeated queries. The common misperception is K V cash — it's not a simple key-value DB in this case, it's the attention cache in the GPU which when warm avoids recompute.
00:02:45 - Rosa: So how do we warm it? We have cold-start patterns every morning.
00:02:49 - Brandon: Prewarming with a scheduled warm-up pass of top queries or synthetic prefixes helps. Also using a small batch of cold queries to amortize kernel startup. Our benchmarks show warm cache hit rates above 80% cut tail by ~35% at p95.
00:03:03 - Avery: Let's talk numbers. If we run 512-d embeddings with 64 candidate rerank and batch size 8 on GPU, what do latency and cost look like?
00:03:12 - Brandon: For a rough micro-benchmark — single NVIDIA A10-ish node: 512-d embedding generation quantized to int8, batch 8 input queries plus 64-candidate dot prods, p50 token gen ~ 18ms, whole rerank ~ 70-110ms depending on kernel warmness. For 1024-d it's closer to 120-180ms.
00:03:35 - Samir: Those 70-110ms numbers — are they with KV cache warmed?
00:03:37 - Brandon: Yes, warm. Cold starts add 40-80ms depending on kernel JIT.
00:03:42 - Maya: Also if you move to dedicated pools you can bound latency more tightly; autoscaling and burst capacity help but dedicated reserved capacity reduces noisy neighbor effects.
00:03:52 - Avery: Cost — can you ballpark per-million embeddings cost for 512-d quantized vs 1024 non-quant?
00:03:59 - Ellen: We usually model cost as compute + storage + network. Very approximate: 512-d quantized (4/8-bit) could be ~ $50-80 per 1M queries in hosted, 1024 non-quant maybe $180-250/1M. On dedicated the unit cost often comes down with commitments but you'd still see 2-3x delta between 512q and 1024fp.
00:04:21 - Devon: On on-prem, our main worry is memory footprint plus GPU count. We have two A100s to start. Can Redwood's private runtime work with our VPC + in-place KMS?
00:04:31 - Maya: Yes we support VPC/private with KMS/HSM integrations; for on-prem we ship a private control plane and runtime manifest. There are some ops adjustments for network egress and image pull. We'll send the private deploy checklist.
00:04:44 - Rosa: Network egress and offline bootstrap are big for us.
00:04:47 - Brandon: Noted. For on-prem with 2xA100, a 512-d quantized model serving dedicated capacity could do ~400-800 qps for pure embed generation depending on batching; rerank with 64 candidates will lower that — think in 40-120 qps range for strict p95 100ms.
00:05:06 - (crosstalk)
00:05:10 - Samir: Do you have any guidance on batch sizing? We see our app-layer batches fluctuate.
00:05:15 - Brandon: Batch sizing guidance: smaller batches reduce tail latency but hurt GPU utilization; larger batches increase throughput but increase p95. For latency SLOs under 120ms, we recommend dynamic batching with max_batch=16 for embed gen and internal grouping for dot-prod compute. If you have a steady 100 rps, aim for batch target 8-12 to optimize for p95.
00:05:35 - Avery: How about quantization formats — 4-bit vs 8-bit? Accuracy tradeoffs?
00:05:39 - Brandon: 4-bit (GPTQ-style) gives best size savings but you can see a slight accuracy hit depending on model. 8-bit is a safe middle ground. We also support hybrid kernels where attention/QK quantize differently. For rerank NDCG we saw <2% drop with 4-bit on some recommendation models, but it's model-dependent.
00:05:59 - Rosa: Any observable differences in latency jitter with quantization?
00:06:03 - Brandon: Quantized kernels can be faster (less memory traffic) and sometimes more predictable. But some 4-bit kernels rely on custom instructions and less mature CUDA paths which can cause jitter on older drivers. We recommend benchmarking on your exact hardware.
00:06:17 - Maya: We'll run the benchmark on your infra. Brandon, can you outline the micro-benchmark you'll run?
00:06:23 - Brandon: Sure: I'll run a 1-hour micro-benchmark using your 24h traces. Steps: 1) replay queries at multiple qps (10/50/100) 2) vary dims {256,512,1024} 3) run quant modes {fp16, int8, 4-bit} 4) measure p50/p95/p99, throughput, GPU util, and KV cache warm vs cold. We'll save results to the benchmark sheet.
00:06:45 - Ellen: I'll share the spreadsheet after the call. link: (drive) https://drive.redwood.example/zenpath-benchmarks (note: placeholder)
00:06:54 - Samir: For rerank, our candidate set is dynamic size 20-200, how do you recommend handling variable candidate counts?
00:07:02 - Brandon: Two options: (A) pad to fixed-size buckets (easier to optimize), or (B) split into micro-batches of candidates so the dot-prod kernels run on compact dense matrices. Padding wastes memory but simplifies runtime. We often use a hybrid: target bucket sizes [32,64,128] and route candidates accordingly.
00:07:22 - Avery: Do you ship an embedding cache that keeps hot vectors?
00:07:26 - Maya: Yes, Redwood has a hot-vector cache layer for embeddings (separate from KV cache). It stores precomputed embeddings of frequent docs and serves them from memory or fast NVMe depending on config. Hit rates of >70% can dramatically cut compute.
00:07:40 - Rosa: How consistent is the cache across old/new model versions? If we roll a new model that slightly shifts vectors, cache invalidation is a mess.
00:07:49 - Brandon: Good point. We provide versioned caches and a migration policy: either recompute cold but staggered, or keep a shadow cache for both versions during rollouts. The Optimize console can estimate cache invalidation cost for N docs.
00:08:02 - Devon: Security — we need audit logs per request and encryption in transit+at-rest.
00:08:08 - Maya: We have request trace logs, audit events, and support KMS/HSM. For Private we can forward logs to your SIEM; we'll include the security pack in the next email.
00:08:20 - (long pause, background noise)
00:08:29 - Samir: Are there any hard limits on vector dims for the ANN indexes? We saw some libs slow after 2048 dims.
00:08:35 - Brandon: Practically you see diminishing returns after 1024 for most semantic search tasks. For ANN indexing, higher dims increase ANN index size & search latency; HNSW scales but memory grows O(n * d). We typically advise max 1024 unless there's clear eval benefit.
00:08:51 - Avery: On the topic of batching and live traffic, what about dynamic batching latency spike mitigation?
00:08:57 - Brandon: Techniques: single-request fast-path, bounded aggregation windows, and early flush if tail latency grows. Also multi-tenant routing to avoid noisy neighbor queues. For very tight SLOs, prefer small dedicated pools.
00:09:10 - Rosa: Are there any specific kernel or driver versions you recommend for stability with 4-bit quant?
00:09:16 - Brandon: Newer CUDA (>=12.x) and patched cuBLAS/cuDNN help. We'll include driver compatibility notes; older driver+OS combos can produce JIT stalls.
00:09:27 - Maya: Let's surface an example cost/latency tradeoff plan: recommended pilot config, expected p95, and cost delta.
00:09:35 - Ellen: Example pilot: 2xA100 private nodes, model: 512-d quantized int8, batch target 8, candidate bucket 64, expected p95 90-110ms, estimated pilot cost (ops + support) for hosted equiv ~$10k/mo or on-prem ops overhead ~ low tens of thousands as a one-time integration. We'll provide a more precise cost model in the spreadsheet.
00:09:56 - Devon: That monthly number seems reasonable. We should validate accuracy/regression on held-out queries.
00:10:00 - Brandon: Absolutely; we'll run evals vs your ground-truth NDCG. We can run A/B or shadow testing.
00:10:07 - Avery: Any red flags we should be aware of?
00:10:10 - Brandon: Main ones: kernel cold-start jitter, cache invalidation during model rollouts, driver incompatibilities for 4-bit kernels, and candidate explosion (very large candidate sets). None are blockers but operational items.
00:10:21 - Maya: Ok, to confirm next steps: Brandon runs micro-benchmark on-prem with your traces, Maya sends security/private deploy docs, Ellen shares benchmark spreadsheet and cost template, ZenPath provides traces and corpus. Any changes?
00:10:36 - Samir: No, that's right.
00:10:38 - Rosa: Timeline ok. We'll try to get trace link today.
00:10:41 - Maya: Great. We'll follow up with calendar invite for POC kickoff 2026-01-22.
00:10:47 - (short pause)
00:10:50 - Brandon: Quick note — if you want to experiment with embedding dims faster, we can stand up a small hosted sandbox for you to run live evals, avoids on-prem setup initially.
00:10:59 - Avery: Might be helpful, yeah.
00:11:02 - Maya: We'll include that as an option in the follow-up email.
00:11:06 - Devon: One more question — does Redwood provide automatic rerank fallback when capacity is constrained? E.g., degrade to cheaper embed-only step.
00:11:15 - Brandon: Yes, we have routing/fallback policies: degrade to CPU-based cheaper model, route to a lighter quantized variant, or reduce candidate set. This is pluggable in rollout policies.
00:11:27 - Maya: Anything else?
00:11:29 - Avery: No, thank you. Very actionable.
00:11:31 - Maya: Thanks all. We'll send email with docs and schedule.
00:11:36 - Meeting end (approx 15:36 UTC).
